questions.question: What is component scanning in Spring Boot?
questions.title: Spring Boot component scanning explained
questions.direct_answer: Component scanning is Spring Boot's automatic bean discovery mechanism. At startup, Spring scans specified packages for classes annotated with @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller, and registers them as beans in the ApplicationContext. This eliminates manual bean configuration XML and enables dependency injection across your application.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands how Spring discovers and registers beans automatically without explicit XML or Java configuration.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Explaining component scanning as just 'finding classes' without mentioning bean registration or the ApplicationContext.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that @SpringBootApplication includes @ComponentScan by default, and explain the package scanning root.

sections.title: Component Scanning: Auto-Discovery of Spring Beans
sections.content:
Component scanning is Spring Boot's mechanism to automatically find and register beans without writing configuration files.

Think of it like a hiring manager scanning resumes — instead of manually calling each candidate, you post the job and qualified applicants (annotated classes) are automatically identified. When Spring Boot starts, it examines the **bytecode** of classes in configured packages, looking for specific annotations like **@Component**, **@Service**, **@Repository**, and **@Controller**. Classes with these annotations are instantiated and registered in the **ApplicationContext** (Spring's bean container), making them available for **dependency injection** throughout your application. This is WHY you can @Autowired a service into a controller without any XML configuration. The @SpringBootApplication annotation on your main class includes @ComponentScan by default, automatically scanning the package containing that main class and all sub-packages.

sections.content:
amber|What it is|~Auto bean discovery|scans bytecode at startup|finds stereotype annotations|no XML wiring
blue|Stereotypes found|~The markers|@Component, @Service|@Repository, @Controller|registered as beans
emerald|ApplicationContext|~The bean container|holds discovered beans|manages lifecycle|enables @Autowired
violet|Scan root|~Where it looks|the main class package|plus all sub-packages|@SpringBootApplication includes it

sections.title: Component Scanning in a Bookstore Application
When Component Scanning Applies
sections.content: Use component scanning in **standard Spring Boot applications** where you want convention-over-configuration and have a clear package structure. It's ideal when building REST APIs, web applications, or microservices where beans follow standard layering (controllers, services, repositories). Component scanning works best when your **packages reflect application layers** (com.example.app.controller, com.example.app.service) and all application code lives under the main class package. However, for **external libraries** or legacy code outside your package tree, you'll need explicit @ComponentScan configuration or @Import to bring in those beans.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Placing the main class in the default package**: If BookstoreApplication sits in the root with no package declaration, Spring can't establish a scan base and won't find any beans. Always use a proper package like com.example.bookstore.
- **Forgetting sub-package scanning rules**: Creating com.example.bookstore.controller and com.example.utilities as sibling packages, then wondering why classes in utilities aren't found — Spring only scans the main package and its children, not siblings.
- **Over-annotating with @Component**: Adding @Component to classes that already have @Service or @Repository, creating redundant annotations since @Service and @Repository are themselves meta-annotated with @Component.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **@SpringBootApplication**: meta-annotation that includes @ComponentScan, @EnableAutoConfiguration, and @Configuration on your main class
- **Stereotype annotations**: @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller are markers that tell Spring to register the class as a bean
- **ApplicationContext**: the Spring container that holds all discovered beans and manages their lifecycle and dependencies
- **Classpath scanning**: Spring uses reflection to examine .class files in configured packages at startup time
- **Default base package**: the package containing @SpringBootApplication plus all descendant packages
- **Dependency injection enablement**: component scanning makes beans available for @Autowired or constructor injection
- **Lazy initialization**: by default all scanned beans are eagerly created at startup unless marked @Lazy

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Component scanning is how Spring Boot automatically discovers and registers your application's beans without writing XML config. When the application starts, Spring examines all classes in the package containing your main class, plus sub-packages, looking for annotations like at-Component, at-Service, at-Repository, or at-Controller. Think of it like Spring going through your codebase with a checklist, finding marked classes and registering them in the ApplicationContext so they can be injected elsewhere. For example, if you've got a BookService class annotated with at-Service in the com.example.bookstore.service package, and your main class with at-SpringBootApplication is in com.example.bookstore, Spring will find that service automatically. You can then inject BookService into a controller using constructor injection, and it just works because both classes were discovered during the scan. One thing freshers often miss — the at-SpringBootApplication annotation already includes at-ComponentScan, so you don't need to add it explicitly. The most common pitfall is putting classes outside the main package tree, like having your main class in com.example.app but utility classes in com.example.shared. Spring won't find those utilities because they're not under the scan root. To fix that, you'd need to explicitly configure at-ComponentScan with additional base packages. The key takeaway is component scanning eliminates boilerplate configuration by using conventions — put your classes in the right packages with the right annotations, and Spring handles the rest.

Without it, you'd register every bean by hand in a config class. That's one line per class, forever. Component scanning kills that boilerplate, so you just drop classes into the right package and move on.

questions.question: What is the difference between @Component, @Service, @Repository, and @Controller?
questions.title: @Component vs @Service vs @Repository vs @Controller
questions.direct_answer: All four annotations register a class as a Spring bean through component scanning. @Service, @Repository, and @Controller are specializations of @Component. The key difference: @Repository adds automatic exception translation from SQL exceptions to Spring's DataAccessException. @Controller integrates with Spring MVC for web handling. @Service is purely semantic with no extra behavior.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows these are all bean registration annotations but understands the functional difference in @Repository exception translation.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying they're 'just for documentation' without knowing @Repository adds exception translation and @Controller has MVC integration.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @Repository, @Service, @Controller are meta-annotated with @Component, and give a concrete example of DataAccessException translation.

sections.title: Stereotype Annotations: Semantic Layering with Functional Differences
sections.content:
These four annotations form Spring's **stereotype hierarchy** for marking beans. At the base is **@Component**, the generic marker that says this class is a Spring-managed bean.

The other three — **@Service**, **@Repository**, and **@Controller** — are specialized versions built on top of @Component through meta-annotation. They all trigger component scanning and bean registration, but they add layer-specific semantics and behavior. @Repository works at the **persistence layer** and adds automatic exception translation, converting database-specific exceptions (like SQLException) into Spring's unified DataAccessException hierarchy. @Controller operates at the **web layer**, integrating with Spring MVC to handle HTTP requests and return views or data. @Service sits in the **business logic layer** and is purely semantic — it has no extra framework behavior but signals intent. This layering helps developers understand code organization at a glance and enables Spring to apply layer-specific features automatically.

sections.title: Stereotype Annotations at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|@Component|~Generic bean|any layer|pure registration|the base annotation
blue|@Service|~Business logic|orchestration layer|semantic only, no extra behavior|signals intent
emerald|@Repository|~Data access|persistence layer|adds exception translation|SQL errors to DataAccessException
violet|@Controller|~Web layer|handles HTTP|MVC request mapping|@RestController adds @ResponseBody

sections.title: Stereotype Annotation Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | @Component | @Service | @Repository | @Controller |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Layer | Generic/any layer | Business logic | Data access | Web/presentation |
| Meta-annotation | Base annotation | Meta-annotated with @Component | Meta-annotated with @Component | Meta-annotated with @Component |
| Extra Behavior | None | None | Exception translation | MVC request mapping |
| Typical Usage | Utility classes | OrderService, PaymentService | OrderRepository, UserDao | BookController, UserController |
| Exception Handling | Standard Java | Standard Java | SQLException to DataAccessException | Standard Java |

sections.title: Stereotypes in a Three-Layer Slice
When to Use Each Annotation
sections.content:
Use **@Repository** for any class that interacts with a database or external data store — JPA repositories, JDBC DAOs, or custom data access objects. The automatic exception translation means you don't have to wrap every database call in try-catch blocks for vendor-specific exceptions.

Use **@Service** for business logic classes that orchestrate operations, apply business rules, or coordinate between repositories and controllers — OrderProcessingService, EmailNotificationService, InventoryService.

Use **@Controller** (or @RestController) for classes that handle HTTP requests in Spring MVC applications — the framework automatically maps request paths to handler methods.

Use plain **@Component** for utility classes, helper beans, or cross-cutting concerns that don't fit the standard three-layer architecture — CacheManager, FileStorageUtil, or custom validators.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @Component everywhere**: Marking a database access class with @Component instead of @Repository means you lose automatic exception translation, and SQLExceptions will bubble up as-is instead of being wrapped in Spring's DataAccessException.
- **Mixing layer annotations**: Putting @Repository on a service class or @Service on a controller confuses the code's intent and might break framework features in future Spring versions that rely on correct stereotype usage.
- **Thinking @Service adds transactions**: Freshers often assume @Service automatically makes methods transactional, but you need explicit @Transactional for that — @Service only registers the bean and signals business logic layer intent.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Meta-annotation hierarchy**: @Service, @Repository, @Controller are all meta-annotated with @Component, inheriting its bean registration behavior
- **@Repository exception translation**: PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor intercepts exceptions from @Repository beans and translates them
- **DataAccessException**: Spring's unified exception hierarchy that wraps vendor-specific database exceptions for consistent error handling
- **@Controller vs @RestController**: @RestController combines @Controller and @ResponseBody, automatically serializing return values to JSON
- **Semantic clarity**: using layer-specific annotations makes code intent explicit and helps developers navigate large codebases
- **AOP pointcuts**: AspectJ expressions can target specific stereotypes, like applying logging to all @Service classes
- **No functional difference for @Service**: it's semantically meaningful but adds zero extra behavior compared to @Component

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: All four annotations tell Spring to register the class as a bean, but they have different purposes and some add extra behavior. At-Component is the base annotation for any Spring-managed class. At-Service, at-Repository, and at-Controller are specialized versions of at-Component, meaning they're meta-annotated with at-Component under the hood. The real difference comes down to layer intent and framework features. At-Repository is for data access classes like JPA repositories or JDBC DAOs. It adds automatic exception translation, which means if your database throws a SQLException, Spring catches it and wraps it in a DataAccessException. This gives you consistent exception handling across different database vendors. At-Service is for business logic — your OrderService or PaymentService classes. It's purely semantic with no extra behavior, but it signals this is where your business rules live. At-Controller is for web layer classes in Spring MVC, handling HTTP requests and returning responses. It integrates with the MVC framework to map URLs to methods. One thing freshers get wrong is thinking these are just documentation or labels. At-Repository genuinely changes behavior with exception translation, and at-Controller enables MVC request handling. Another mistake is using at-Component for everything because you don't see an immediate difference. But if you mark a repository with at-Component, you lose the exception translation feature. The takeaway is these annotations reflect the three-layer architecture — controllers for web, services for logic, repositories for data — and at-Repository adds real exception handling value.

speakable_v2.hook: All four register a bean — but @Repository does something extra that the others don't.
speakable_v2.standard_example: A @Repository DAO whose SQLException becomes a DataAccessException

beats.text: All four mark a class as a Spring bean, so component scan picks them up. The base is @Component. The other three are just @Component wearing a role: @Service, @Repository, and @Controller.

Reach for @Repository on data access classes, where you get exception translation for free. Use @Controller for web endpoints. @Service marks business logic. Plain @Component fits the odd helper class.
Mark a DAO with @Repository and a raw SQLException turns into a Spring DataAccessException. The gotcha: swap in @Component there and you'll lose that for free wrapping.

speakable_v2.cap: So they're all beans under the hood. The labels just show intent. Only @Repository adds something real.

questions.question: What is the default component scan base package in Spring Boot?
questions.title: Default component scan package in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: The default scan base is the package containing the @SpringBootApplication class, plus all its sub-packages. If your main class is in com.example.bookstore, Spring scans com.example.bookstore.service, com.example.bookstore.repository, etc., but NOT sibling packages like com.example.utils. This is why 'bean not found' errors happen when components are outside the main package tree.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the component scan root and can troubleshoot common 'bean not found' issues caused by package structure.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking Spring scans the entire project or all com.example packages, not realizing it's anchored to the main class package.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @SpringBootApplication includes @ComponentScan, and mention how to override the base packages if needed.

sections.title: Default Scan Base: Main Class Package as the Root
sections.content:
Spring Boot's default component scan base is the **package of the class annotated with @SpringBootApplication**, plus all packages nested beneath it in the hierarchy. This is a convention-over-configuration design: put your main application class at the root of your module structure, and everything below it gets scanned automatically.

If BookstoreApplication sits in **com.example.bookstore**, Spring scans com.example.bookstore itself, plus com.example.bookstore.controller, com.example.bookstore.service, com.example.bookstore.repository, and any other sub-packages like com.example.bookstore.config.security. However, it does NOT scan sibling packages such as com.example.utils or com.other.library — those are outside the scan tree. This anchoring to the main class package is WHY the most common fresher mistake is a "bean not found" error: they create a class in the wrong package location, outside the scan root, and Spring never registers it. Understanding this hierarchy is critical for debugging dependency injection failures and structuring multi-module projects correctly.

sections.title: Default Scan Base Package at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Scan root|~Anchored to main class|package of @SpringBootApplication|the starting point|convention over config
blue|Goes down|~Children included|sub-packages scanned|deeper nesting too|controller, service, repository
rose|Not sideways|~Siblings excluded|com.example.utils skipped|outside the tree|cause of 'bean not found'
emerald|Fix|~Place main at the root|or set scanBasePackages|or add @ComponentScan|keep everything below main

sections.title: Component Scan Base Package Structure
When Default Scanning Works Perfectly
sections.content: The default scan base works perfectly for **monolithic Spring Boot applications** where all your code lives in a single module with a clear package hierarchy. If you're building a REST API with standard layers (controllers, services, repositories, config) all under com.company.productname, the default scanning requires zero configuration. It also works well for **single-module Maven or Gradle projects** where the main class sits at the package root and all feature packages branch from there. The pattern shines in **greenfield projects** where you can design the package structure from scratch following Spring Boot conventions. However, it breaks down in **multi-module projects**, when integrating **third-party library beans**, or when **refactoring legacy code** that has non-standard package structures — those cases need explicit @ComponentScan configuration.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Creating the main class in the default package**: Putting BookstoreApplication in the root with no package declaration means Spring has no base to scan from, and no beans will be found. Always declare a package like com.example.bookstore.
- **Assuming Spring scans the entire src folder**: Freshers think Spring scans everything under src/main/java, but it only scans the main class package tree. Creating com.example.bookstore and com.example.shared as sibling packages means shared won't be scanned.
- **Misunderstanding multi-module projects**: In a Maven multi-module setup with bookstore-api and bookstore-service modules, each has its own scan root. Beans in bookstore-service won't be visible to bookstore-api without explicit configuration or shared parent package.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Scan root anchor**: the package containing the @SpringBootApplication class is the starting point for component scanning
- **Hierarchical scanning**: Spring scans the root package plus all descendant packages, following the dot-separated package tree structure
- **Sibling exclusion**: packages at the same level as the main package are NOT scanned — only children and deeper descendants
- **@ComponentScan default**: when you don't specify basePackages on @ComponentScan, it defaults to the package of the annotated class
- **Multi-module considerations**: in multi-module projects, each module with a @SpringBootApplication has its own scan root
- **Bean not found errors**: 90% of 'required bean not found' errors in fresh projects are caused by classes outside the scan tree
- **Convention over configuration**: the default behavior eliminates XML and reduces boilerplate when following standard package layouts

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The default component scan base package is wherever your at-SpringBootApplication class lives, plus all packages underneath it. So if your main application class is in com.example.bookstore, Spring will scan that package and everything nested below it — like com.example.bookstore.controller, com.example.bookstore.service, and so on. But it won't scan sibling packages like com.example.utils or com.other.anything, because those are outside the scan tree. Think of it like a folder hierarchy — Spring starts at the main class folder and goes down into all subfolders, but it doesn't go sideways to neighboring folders. This is why package structure matters so much in Spring Boot. If you create a service class in a package that's not under the main class package, Spring won't find it, and you'll get a 'bean not found' error at startup. For example, if your main class is in com.example.app but you put a utility class in com.example.helpers as a sibling, that helper won't be scanned. The most common mistake freshers make is putting the main class in the wrong place or not understanding this parent-child package relationship. Another pitfall is thinking Spring scans the entire src slash main slash java directory — it doesn't, it only scans from the main class package down. The default behavior comes from at-SpringBootApplication, which includes at-ComponentScan without explicit base packages. If you need to scan additional packages outside the default tree, you can override it by adding at-ComponentScan with base packages specified, but for most single-module applications, the default just works if you structure your packages correctly.

questions.question: How do you configure component scanning to include additional packages?
questions.title: Configuring @ComponentScan base packages
questions.direct_answer: Use @ComponentScan(basePackages = {"com.example.myapp", "com.other.util"}) on your @SpringBootApplication class to add packages outside the default scan path. Alternatively, use @ComponentScan(basePackageClasses = {MyMarker.class, UtilMarker.class}) to reference marker classes whose packages should be scanned. This is type-safe and refactoring-friendly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows how to configure Spring when the default package structure doesn't fit the project needs.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing about @ComponentScan at all, or suggesting moving all code into one package instead of configuring the scan.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention basePackageClasses as the type-safe alternative to string-based basePackages configuration.

sections.title: Overriding Component Scan: Adding External Packages to the Scan Path
sections.content:
When the default component scan base doesn't cover all your beans — such as shared utility packages, third-party library components, or multi-module project dependencies — you configure additional scan paths using **@ComponentScan** on your @SpringBootApplication class. Spring provides two approaches: **basePackages** uses string package names like "com.other.library", while **basePackageClasses** references actual Java classes as type-safe markers for their packages.

The basePackageClasses approach is preferred because it survives refactoring — if you rename a package, the compiler catches the broken reference, whereas string-based packages silently break. When you add @ComponentScan, you're extending Spring's search scope beyond the main class package tree to include additional roots. This is common in **multi-module Maven projects** where shared modules sit outside your application module's package hierarchy, or when integrating **legacy code** that can't be restructured to fit Spring Boot conventions.

sections.title: Configuring Extra Scan Packages at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|When|~Beans outside the tree|shared utility modules|third-party beans|multi-module projects
blue|basePackages|~String names|@ComponentScan(basePackages=...)|fragile to renames|silent failure on a typo
emerald|basePackageClasses|~Type-safe markers|reference a class per package|refactor-friendly|compiler catches breaks
rose|The trap|~Override replaces the default|main package no longer auto-scanned|add it back explicitly|or your own beans vanish

sections.title: Configuring Additional Component Scan Packages
When to Configure Additional Scan Packages
sections.content:
Use explicit @ComponentScan configuration in **multi-module Maven/Gradle projects** where a shared-utils module with package com.company.shared needs to be scanned by an api module with package com.company.api — they're sibling packages, so the default won't find shared. Configure it when **integrating third-party Spring-based libraries** that provide @Component-annotated beans in their own package space, like a custom authentication library or a shared service framework.

Use it for **legacy codebases** being migrated to Spring Boot where existing package structures can't be refactored to nest under the main application package. However, if you're building a **greenfield single-module application**, restructure your packages to fit the default convention instead of adding configuration — move utility classes into com.company.app.util rather than keeping them in com.company.utils.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting to include the default package**: When you specify @ComponentScan(basePackages = {"com.other.util"}), you override the default behavior entirely, and Spring stops scanning com.example.myapp where your main class lives. You must explicitly include the main package in the array.
- **Using basePackages with typos**: Writing @ComponentScan(basePackages = "com.exmple.utils") with a typo silently breaks scanning — no compile error, just missing beans at runtime. This is why basePackageClasses is safer.
- **Over-scanning with root packages**: Configuring basePackages = {"com"} makes Spring scan every package starting with com, including all third-party libraries, dramatically slowing startup time. Be specific with package paths to only scan what you need.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **@ComponentScan override**: adding @ComponentScan to @SpringBootApplication replaces the default behavior, so include all needed packages
- **basePackages attribute**: accepts String array of package names to scan, straightforward but fragile during refactoring
- **basePackageClasses attribute**: accepts Class array where each class's package becomes a scan root, type-safe and refactor-friendly
- **Marker interface pattern**: create empty interfaces as package markers for basePackageClasses, commonly named PackageMarker or PackageInfo
- **Scan performance**: more packages and deeper hierarchies increase startup time, only scan what's necessary
- **Combines with default**: you can use both basePackages and basePackageClasses together in the same annotation
- **Multi-module projects**: each module with @SpringBootApplication needs explicit @ComponentScan to find beans in other modules

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To include additional packages in component scanning, you add the at-ComponentScan annotation to your at-SpringBootApplication class. There are two ways to do it. First, you can use base packages with an array of package name strings, like at-ComponentScan base packages equals open brace quote com dot example dot myapp quote comma quote com dot other dot util quote close brace. This tells Spring to scan both packages and their sub-packages. The second way, which is better, is using base package classes. Instead of strings, you provide actual Java classes from the packages you want to scan. For example, at-ComponentScan base package classes equals open brace MyMarker dot class comma UtilMarker dot class close brace. Spring scans the package containing each of those marker classes. The marker classes are usually empty interfaces you create just to mark the package — they don't need any methods or fields. Why is base package classes better? Because it's type-safe. If you rename a package, the compiler will catch the broken class reference, but with string-based base packages, you get a silent failure at runtime. One critical mistake freshers make is forgetting that when you add at-ComponentScan, you override the default behavior. If you only specify other packages, Spring stops scanning your main application package. So you need to include your main package in the list too, or reference your main application class in base package classes. For example, at-ComponentScan base package classes equals open brace BookstoreApplication dot class comma SharedUtilsMarker dot class close brace keeps both the default and adds the new one. This configuration is common in multi-module projects where you have separate Maven modules with different package roots, or when using shared utility libraries that aren't nested under your application package.

speakable_v2.hook: When components live outside the default scan path, you override @ComponentScan — but there's a trap worth knowing.

beats.text: Configuring component scan means telling Spring to look in extra packages beyond the default. You add @ComponentScan to your main class and list the packages, or point at marker classes, so Spring widens its search.
Sometimes your beans live outside the main package tree. Shared modules, third-party libraries, or legacy code won't sit under your root. @ComponentScan lets you pull those packages in too.

items: basePackages takes string package names, which is quick but breaks quietly on a typo.
basePackageClasses points at a class per package, so renames stay safe and the compiler checks them.
Both can combine, and you list as many roots as you need.

beats.text: Add @ComponentScan with basePackages for com.example.shop and com.shared.utils. Both get scanned now. Here's the non-obvious part. The moment you set basePackages, the default root drops out, so your own main package needs listing again.

items: Forgetting to relist your main package after setting basePackages, so your own beans vanish.
Typing a package name wrong, which fails silently instead of at compile time.

speakable_v2.cap: So override only when beans live elsewhere. Prefer basePackageClasses, and always keep your main package in the list.

questions.question: What is the difference between @Component and @Bean?
questions.title: @Component vs @Bean in Spring
questions.direct_answer: @Component is a class-level annotation that marks your own classes for automatic detection during component scanning. @Bean is a method-level annotation in @Configuration classes where you write a factory method that produces and returns a bean instance. Use @Component for your code; use @Bean for third-party classes you can't annotate, or when you need complex instantiation logic.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands Spring's two distinct bean registration mechanisms and when to use each.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing the two or not realizing @Bean gives you programmatic control over instantiation and configuration.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @Bean methods can accept parameters (dependencies) and return any type, while @Component only works on classes you own.

sections.title: Two Ways to Register Beans in Spring
sections.content:
Spring Boot offers two primary mechanisms to register beans in the ApplicationContext. **@Component** is a class-level stereotype annotation you put directly on your own Java classes — Spring's component scanner finds these classes at startup and automatically creates beans from them. **@Bean** is a method-level annotation you use inside **@Configuration** classes to define a factory method that produces a bean — you write the instantiation code yourself.

The key difference: @Component is declarative (Spring creates the instance for you), while @Bean is programmatic (you control exactly how the object is created). Think of @Component as "Spring, make a bean from this class" and @Bean as "Spring, call this method to get a bean." You need @Bean when working with third-party library classes you can't modify to add @Component, or when bean creation requires complex logic like conditional instantiation, multiple constructor arguments, or post-construction setup.

sections.title: @Component vs @Bean at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|@Component|~On your classes|class-level annotation|found by component scan|Spring calls the constructor
blue|@Bean|~In @Configuration|method-level factory|you write the creation logic|Spring registers the return value
emerald|Use @Component|~Code you own|services, repositories|simple instantiation|just annotate
violet|Use @Bean|~Code you don't own|RestTemplate, ObjectMapper|complex or conditional setup|params get injected

sections.title: @Component vs @Bean Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | @Component | @Bean |
|---|---|---|
| Applied to | Class definition you own | Method in @Configuration class |
| Detection | Automatic via component scanning | Explicit method invocation by Spring |
| Use case | Your application classes | Third-party classes or complex setup |
| Instantiation control | Spring controls construction | You write the factory method |
| Dependency injection | Via constructor or field injection | Via method parameters |

sections.title: Using @Component and @Bean Together
When to Use Each Approach
sections.content: **Use @Component** for your own application classes: services, repositories, controllers, and components you write from scratch. It's the simplest approach — just annotate the class and Spring Boot's component scanning finds it automatically. **Use @Bean** when you need to register third-party library classes as beans (like Jackson's ObjectMapper, Apache HttpClient, or database connection pools) because you can't add @Component to code you don't own. Also use @Bean when bean creation requires complex logic: conditional instantiation based on properties, multiple constructor arguments that need custom values, or post-construction configuration like setting timeouts or registering modules. Finally, use @Bean when you need to create multiple beans of the same type with different configurations — you can't do that with @Component.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @Component on third-party classes**: Freshers try to annotate library classes they don't control, which obviously fails. You can only put @Component on source code you write yourself — for everything else, use @Bean in a configuration class.
- **Mixing @Bean and @Component on the same class**: Some freshers annotate a class with both, thinking it provides "extra registration." Spring will create two separate bean instances, causing confusing behavior and duplicate beans. Choose one approach per class.
- **Not understanding @Bean method parameters**: Freshers write @Bean methods with hardcoded dependencies instead of accepting parameters. Spring automatically injects dependencies as method parameters — this is how @Bean methods declare their own dependencies in a clean, testable way.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **@Component**: class-level annotation for your own classes, detected automatically by component scanning
- **@Bean**: method-level annotation in @Configuration classes where you write a factory method that returns a bean instance
- **@Component variants**: @Service, @Repository, @Controller are specialized @Component annotations with semantic meaning
- **@Bean use cases**: third-party classes, complex instantiation logic, multiple beans of the same type with different configs
- **@Bean parameters**: Spring injects dependencies as method parameters, enabling clean declarative dependency management
- **Scanning vs explicit**: @Component relies on @ComponentScan, @Bean methods are always invoked regardless of scan configuration
- **Control**: @Bean gives you full programmatic control over object creation, @Component delegates to Spring's default instantiation

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I'd say the main difference is where you apply them and who controls instantiation. At Component is a class-level annotation you put on your own classes like services or repositories. Spring's component scanner finds these classes at startup and automatically creates beans from them. You use it when you're writing your own application code and want Spring to manage it. At Bean is a method-level annotation you use inside an at-Configuration class. You write a factory method that produces and returns the bean instance, so you control exactly how it's created. This is essential when you're working with third-party library classes you can't modify, like Jackson's ObjectMapper or Apache's HttpClient. You can't add at Component to those because you don't own the source code. At Bean also lets you do complex setup — maybe you need to set timeouts, register modules, or configure the object in ways that require multiple steps. The method can accept parameters for dependencies, and Spring injects them automatically. So if I'm building an OrderService that's my own code, I'd use at Component. But if I need to configure an ObjectMapper with custom settings, I'd write a at Bean method in a configuration class. One mistake freshers make is trying to use both on the same class, which creates duplicate beans. Just pick the right tool: at Component for your classes, at Bean for everything else or when you need fine-grained control.

speakable_v2.hook: @Component and @Bean both register beans — but they solve different problems and you need to know which to reach for.
speakable_v2.standard_example: A RestTemplate built in a @Bean method while services use @Component
speakable_v2.familiarity_override_reason: This compares @Component and @Bean, so the codex bean-lifecycle example doesn't fit the tiny example beat.

beats.text: @Component sits on a class you own, and component scan turns it into a bean. A @Bean method inside a @Configuration class does the same job by hand. Either way @PostConstruct runs after dependency injection, since both end up managed beans.

Pick @Component for classes you write, like services and repositories. Pick @Bean for types you cannot annotate, like RestTemplate or ObjectMapper. Reach for it too when building one needs real setup. Don't put both on one class.
Configure a RestTemplate with a @Bean method and Spring registers what it returns. The gotcha: mark that same class @Component too and you'll get two beans fighting.

speakable_v2.cap: So @Component's for your code, and @Bean's for everything else. One class, one path. Pick the right tool and you're set.

questions.question: What is bean scope in Spring and what are the common scopes?
questions.title: Spring bean scopes — singleton vs prototype
questions.direct_answer: Bean scope controls the lifecycle and number of instances Spring creates. Singleton (default) means one shared instance per ApplicationContext. Prototype means a new instance every time the bean is requested. Web scopes include request (one per HTTP request) and session (one per HTTP session). Most application beans are singleton because they're stateless services or repositories.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands that singleton is the default, what it means, and when you'd need a different scope.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Spring singleton with the Gang of Four singleton pattern, or not realizing most beans are shared instances.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the thread-safety implication of singleton scope and why stateless design matters for shared beans.

sections.title: Bean Scope Controls Instance Lifecycle
sections.content:
**Bean scope** defines how many instances of a bean Spring creates and how long they live. It's a fundamental concept because Spring's default behavior is to create only one instance of each bean and share it across the entire application.

The **singleton scope** (default) means Spring creates exactly one instance per ApplicationContext and reuses that same instance every time the bean is injected or requested. This is different from the classic Singleton design pattern — Spring singleton is scoped to the container, not the JVM. **Prototype scope** means Spring creates a new instance every time you ask for the bean. There are also **web scopes** (request, session, application) that tie bean lifecycle to HTTP constructs. Think of scope as answering "how many instances should exist and when should they be recreated?" For example, a singleton OrderService instance handles requests from all users concurrently, while a prototype scope bean like a ShoppingCart might need a fresh instance per user or operation. Understanding scope is critical because it affects thread safety, memory usage, and how you design your beans.

sections.title: Bean Scopes at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|singleton|~Default scope|one per ApplicationContext|shared everywhere|must be stateless
blue|prototype|~New each request|fresh instance per lookup|you handle cleanup|no destroy callback
emerald|request|~Per HTTP request|web context only|correlation IDs, context|dies with the request
violet|session|~Per HTTP session|across requests, one user|carts, preferences|web context only

sections.title: Declaring Bean Scopes in Spring Boot
Choosing the Right Scope
sections.content: **Use singleton scope** (the default) for stateless services, repositories, controllers, and utility classes — basically 95% of your beans. These beans don't store user-specific data in fields, so one shared instance is safe and memory-efficient. Examples: OrderService, CustomerRepository, EmailSender. **Use prototype scope** when you need a new instance with fresh state each time, like a report generator that accumulates data during processing, or a task executor that maintains operation-specific state. Be careful — prototype beans are never garbage collected until all references are released. **Use request scope** for beans that hold request-specific data like correlation IDs, user context, or request metadata that should live only for one HTTP request. **Use session scope** for beans that store user session data like shopping carts or user preferences that persist across multiple requests from the same user. Most backend APIs use singleton for services and repositories, with request scope occasionally for context objects.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Storing mutable state in singleton beans**: Freshers add fields like currentUser or orderList to singleton services, not realizing that field is shared across all threads and users. Singleton beans must be stateless or use thread-safe collections. Any mutable state should be method-local or externalized to a database.
- **Confusing Spring singleton with JVM singleton**: Spring singleton means one instance per ApplicationContext, not per JVM. If you run multiple Spring Boot apps in the same JVM (rare), each has its own singleton instances. The Gang of Four Singleton pattern uses a private constructor and static instance, but Spring singleton is managed by the container with no such restrictions.
- **Prototype scope memory leaks**: Freshers create prototype beans but never release references, assuming Spring will garbage collect them. Spring creates the instance and hands it to you — you're responsible for cleanup. Prototype beans don't have a destroy callback unless you explicitly configure one.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Singleton scope**: default, one shared instance per ApplicationContext, reused across all injections and requests
- **Prototype scope**: new instance created every time the bean is requested from the container
- **Request scope**: one instance per HTTP request, destroyed when request completes, requires web context
- **Session scope**: one instance per HTTP session, persists across multiple requests from same user
- **Thread safety**: singleton beans must be stateless or use thread-safe data structures, since they're shared across threads
- **@Scope annotation**: use @Scope("singleton") or @Scope("prototype") on @Component/@Service/@Bean to declare scope
- **Memory implications**: singleton is memory-efficient, prototype can cause memory leaks if instances aren't released

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Bean scope controls how many instances Spring creates and how long they live. The default scope is singleton, which means Spring creates exactly one instance per ApplicationContext and shares that instance everywhere it's injected. So if you have an OrderService bean, there's just one OrderService object handling all requests from all users. That's why singleton beans need to be stateless — they can't store user-specific data in fields because multiple threads access the same instance concurrently. Most of your beans will be singleton because services and repositories don't hold state; they just process data and call other beans. Prototype scope is the opposite: Spring creates a new instance every time you ask for the bean. You'd use this for something like a report generator that accumulates data during processing and needs fresh state each time. There are also web scopes like request and session. Request scope means one instance per HTTP request, which is useful for storing request-specific context like correlation IDs. Session scope means one instance per user session, good for shopping carts or user preferences. One common mistake is putting mutable fields in singleton beans, like a list of orders. That list is shared across all users, causing data corruption. Keep singleton beans stateless or use thread-safe collections. Another mistake is confusing Spring singleton with the classic Singleton pattern — Spring's is scoped to the container, not the JVM, and doesn't use private constructors or static instances.

speakable_v2.hook: Singleton is the default scope — and it means all @Service beans are shared. That's why they must be stateless.
speakable_v2.standard_example: A singleton @Service shared across concurrent requests

beats.text: Bean scope decides how many copies of a bean Spring makes and how long each lives. The default is singleton, and singleton means one per ApplicationContext, not per JVM. Every injection shares it.
Most beans are stateless services, so sharing one copy saves memory. But some beans hold per-request or per-user state. Scopes let you match a bean's lifetime to how the app uses it.

items: Singleton, the default, gives one shared instance per ApplicationContext.
Prototype hands you a fresh instance on every request for the bean.
Request scope lives for a single HTTP request, while session scope spans one user session.

beats.text: Take a singleton OrderService handling every request at once. Here's the non-obvious part. If you stash a field like currentUser, two requests overwrite each other. That's why singleton beans stay stateless.

items: Storing mutable state in a singleton, which concurrent requests then corrupt.
Mixing up Spring singleton with the Gang of Four pattern, which it is not.

speakable_v2.cap: So pick scope by lifetime. Keep singletons stateless, and reach for prototype or web scopes only when state demands it.

questions.question: What is @Autowired and how does Spring resolve which bean to inject?
questions.title: @Autowired and Spring dependency injection
questions.direct_answer: @Autowired tells Spring to inject a dependency automatically. Spring resolves it by type first: it looks for a bean whose type matches the field, parameter, or setter. If multiple beans of that type exist, Spring resolves by name (matching the field name to a bean name). Use @Qualifier("beanName") to explicitly specify which bean to inject when there's ambiguity.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands Spring's dependency injection resolution mechanism and can troubleshoot ambiguous injection scenarios.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the by-type-then-by-name resolution order, or not understanding when @Qualifier is needed.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that constructor injection is preferred over field injection, and explain why (testability, immutability).

sections.title: Spring's Automatic Dependency Injection
sections.content:
**@Autowired** is Spring's annotation for automatic dependency injection — it tells the container to find and inject a bean into a field, constructor parameter, or setter method. This eliminates manual instantiation and wiring, letting Spring manage object dependencies.

When Spring encounters @Autowired, it follows a two-step resolution process. **First, it resolves by type**: Spring looks in the ApplicationContext for a bean whose type matches the declared type of the field or parameter. If exactly one bean of that type exists, Spring injects it — done. **Second, if multiple beans of the same type exist** (like two DataSource beans or multiple PaymentProcessor implementations), Spring resolves by name: it matches the field or parameter name to a bean name (usually the class name with lowercase first letter). If ambiguity remains, Spring throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException at startup. You use **@Qualifier("beanName")** to explicitly specify which bean to inject when there's ambiguity. Think of @Autowired as "Spring, find the dependency I need and give it to me," with type being the primary key and name as the tiebreaker.

sections.title: How @Autowired Resolves a Bean
sections.content:
amber|Step 1: by type|~Match the declared type|one bean of that type|inject it, done|the primary key
blue|Step 2: by name|~Multiple candidates|match field/param name|to a bean name|the tiebreaker
emerald|@Qualifier / @Primary|~Break the tie|@Qualifier("beanName") is explicit|@Primary sets a default|else NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException
violet|Constructor injection|~Preferred style|final fields, immutable|testable without Spring|optional on a single constructor

sections.title: Dependency Injection with @Autowired
When and How to Use @Autowired
sections.content: **Use constructor injection** (preferred): declare a constructor with dependencies as parameters. Spring calls this constructor and injects beans. As of Spring 4.3, @Autowired is optional on single constructors, so you can omit it for cleaner code. Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit, enables immutability (final fields), and makes testing easier because you can instantiate the class without Spring. **Use field injection** for quick prototypes or simple cases: annotate the field directly with @Autowired. It's concise but makes testing harder (you need reflection to set dependencies in tests) and hides required dependencies from the API. **Use @Qualifier** when you have multiple beans of the same type: add @Qualifier("beanName") alongside @Autowired to tell Spring exactly which bean to inject. Common scenarios include multiple DataSource beans for different databases, or multiple API client implementations for different vendors. **Avoid @Autowired(required=false)** unless you genuinely want an optional dependency — it makes your code fragile and error-prone.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using field injection everywhere**: Freshers use field injection because it's shortest, but it makes classes hard to test without Spring's test framework and violates encapsulation. Constructor injection is preferred because it makes dependencies explicit and allows plain Java object instantiation in tests.
- **Not understanding by-type-then-by-name resolution**: When injection fails with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException, freshers don't realize they can either use @Qualifier or rename their field to match a bean name. If you have beans named customerService and orderService, a field named customerService will resolve to the matching bean by name.
- **Circular dependencies with field injection**: Freshers create circular dependencies (A depends on B, B depends on A) which Spring can sometimes resolve with field injection but fails with constructor injection. This masks a design problem — circular dependencies indicate you need to refactor into a third service.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **@Autowired**: tells Spring to automatically inject a bean into a field, constructor parameter, or setter method
- **Resolution by type**: Spring first looks for a bean whose type matches the declared type of the injection point
- **Resolution by name**: if multiple beans of the same type exist, Spring matches the field/parameter name to a bean name
- **@Qualifier**: explicitly specifies which bean to inject when there's ambiguity, used alongside @Autowired
- **Constructor injection**: preferred approach, enables immutability with final fields and makes testing easier without Spring
- **Field injection**: convenient but makes testing harder and hides dependencies, use constructor injection instead
- **NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException**: thrown at startup when multiple beans match and Spring can't resolve which one to inject

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: At Autowired tells Spring to automatically inject a dependency for you. You put it on a field, constructor, or setter, and Spring finds the right bean and injects it. The resolution process works in two steps. First, Spring looks for a bean by type — it searches the ApplicationContext for a bean whose type matches what you declared. If there's exactly one bean of that type, Spring injects it and you're done. But if there are multiple beans of the same type, like two PaymentProcessor implementations, Spring resolves by name. It matches your field name or parameter name to a bean name. So if your field is named stripeProcessor and there's a bean with that name, Spring injects it. If Spring still can't decide, it throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException at startup. That's when you use at Qualifier. You add at Qualifier with the bean name next to at Autowired to tell Spring exactly which bean you want. For example, at Qualifier stripe payment processor next to a PaymentProcessor parameter. Now, constructor injection is preferred over field injection. With constructor injection, you declare a constructor that takes dependencies as parameters, and Spring calls it. This lets you make fields final for immutability and makes testing way easier because you can just new up the class in a test without Spring. Field injection is convenient but it hides dependencies and makes testing harder. One mistake freshers make is not understanding the by-type-then-by-name order. They get the NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException and don't realize they can fix it with at Qualifier or by renaming the field to match a bean name.

speakable_v2.hook: @Autowired resolves by type — but when there are multiple candidates, you need to know how to break the tie.

beats.text: @Autowired tells Spring to inject a dependency for you. You put it on a field, constructor, or setter, and Spring finds the matching bean and wires it in automatically.
Without it, you'd wire every dependency by hand. @Autowired lets Spring own that plumbing, so your classes just declare what they need and trust the container to supply it.

items: First Spring resolves by type, looking for one bean that matches the field.
If several match, it falls back to the field name to break the tie.
Still stuck, it throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException unless @Qualifier or @Primary picks one.

beats.text: Say two PaymentProcessor beans exist, Stripe and PayPal. Inject by type alone and Spring can't choose. Here's the non-obvious part. Add @Qualifier with the bean name, or mark one @Primary, and the tie breaks.

items: Leaning on field injection, which hides dependencies and makes testing harder.
Forgetting the type-then-name order, so an ambiguous injection looks random.

speakable_v2.cap: So @Autowired matches by type first, then name. Prefer constructor injection, and break ties with @Qualifier or @Primary.
